opus-5.5.text:
Realism matters, but I don't think it's a single dial you turn all the way up. It depends on what the world is for.

Take a game designer, a filmmaker, or an architect sketching a concept. They often want something stylized, something that has never existed. For them, photorealism isn't the point. What matters is that the world is coherent: when you move the camera, the geometry holds; when you look behind an object, something sensible is there; the lighting behaves consistently. That kind of spatial and physical consistency is, in a way, a deeper form of realism than surface appearance.

Then there are use cases where fidelity to the real world is essential. If you're training a robot, building simulations for manufacturing, or doing anything in healthcare, the physics, materials, and dynamics need to be right. A beautiful world that gets friction or object permanence wrong is worse than useless there, because it teaches the wrong lessons.

So the way I frame it is that the foundation has to be spatial intelligence. The model has to understand the 3D structure of the world, how things relate in space, and how they change over time. If you get that right, you can generate worlds anywhere along the spectrum, from hyperreal to fantastical, and they'll still feel *right* to a human or be useful to a machine.

Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years building perception and action around a 3D world. Our models are just starting that journey. Visual realism is the part that impresses people first, but structural realism is what makes these worlds truly useful.

r001.rationale: The response says worlds can be fantastical or stylized yet remain coherent and still feel right.

r002.rationale: It calls spatial intelligence the foundation and describes understanding 3D structure and spatial relationships as central to it.

fable-5.1.text:
Realism is a word I actually try to be careful with, because people hear it and immediately think photorealism, and that's only one slice of what matters.

When I think about world models, I think about what the world has to afford, not just how it looks. If you're building a world for an agent to act in, the thing that matters is whether the geometry is consistent, whether objects persist when you look away, whether the physics behaves in a way that lets you plan. A world can be rendered beautifully and still be useless if the chair you set a cup on doesn't actually hold it, or if walking around a corner changes what was on the other side. So I'd say the first order of realism is structural and physical coherence. That's what the brain actually relies on. Evolution didn't optimize us for pixels, it optimized us for being able to predict what happens when we push on something.

Visual fidelity matters too, but in a more context-dependent way. If you're training a robot that's going to be deployed in a real kitchen, you want the sensory distribution to be close enough that the sim-to-real gap is manageable. If you're building a space for a designer to sketch ideas, or for a scientist to run a thought experiment, a stylized world might be exactly right. So I don't think of realism as a single dial you turn up as high as possible. It's a set of properties, and the question is always, realistic with respect to what task, and for whom?

The other thing I'd add is that humans are remarkably good at living in imperfect worlds. We read novels, we play video games, we look at Cézanne. What we can't tolerate is incoherence. If a world violates its own rules, our sense of being somewhere collapses. So in the work we're doing at World Labs, that's the bar I care most about: can a person or an agent inhabit this space, move through it, interact with it, and have it hold together? If you get that right, you've captured the part of realism that actually matters for intelligence. The rest is engineering, and it's getting better quickly.

r001.rationale: The response says stylized worlds can suit some tasks and emphasizes coherence, but it does not clearly state that an AI-generated 3D world can be fantastical while remaining plausible.

r002.rationale: It identifies consistent geometry, persistent objects, and coherent physics as the first-order realism an agent needs to act and plan, and says this coherence matters for intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think realism has to be connected to what you want the world model to do. If you’re using it to train a robot, a beautiful image is not enough. When the robot pushes an object, does it move in a physically plausible way? Does the object stay where you left it when you turn away and look back? That consistency is a very important part of realism.

And then there’s visual realism, which matters a great deal for some applications. But you could also imagine a stylized world that is incredibly useful for creating, exploring, or learning. It doesn’t have to look like a photograph to have coherent spatial relationships.

So I would frame the question around what properties of the world we need to preserve. Appearance is one. Geometry, physics, and how the world responds to your actions are others. The deeper challenge is bringing those together so that a model can support interaction, rather than just produce something that looks convincing for a moment.

r001.rationale: It says a world can be stylized rather than photorealistic while retaining coherent spatial relationships and physically plausible behavior, conveying that non-realistic appearance can coexist with plausibility.

r002.rationale: It describes spatial relationships, geometry, and physics as important properties, but does not connect spatial plausibility to spatial intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think realism is important, but we have to ask: realism for what? If you’re creating a world for entertainment, you might care a lot about visual fidelity. But if you want an agent to learn how to act in that world, a beautiful image is not enough. You need the world to behave consistently. Objects need to persist when you look away. Actions need to have consequences that make physical sense.

And realism doesn’t mean every world has to look like a photograph. You can have a very stylized world that still has coherent geometry and physics. So I would separate appearance from the underlying structure of the world. The level of detail you need depends on the task, but that consistency becomes very important if you want intelligence that can reason, plan, and interact.

r001.rationale: The response says a stylized world can have coherent geometry and physics, but does not clearly state that a fantastical world can remain plausible.

r002.rationale: It says coherent geometry, physics, and consistent world behavior are very important for intelligence that can reason, plan, and interact.
